headline:
It works, and it is 804 lines. Rectangles on R, lines on L, arrows on A, drawn by dragging on an infinite canvas — plus select, hand-pan, delete, and arrows that bind to a rectangle and follow it when you move it. Public and MIT at zacharyyamaoka/simple-reactflow-whiteboard.

The reference you named is the wrong one. openflowkit is 122,574 lines and does not do this: every shape is a fixed-size palette add on double-click, every edge is handle-to-handle, and there are no R/L/A bindings at all. Your own pyblocks whiteboard is the real prior art, and this repo is ported from it.

openflowkit is a node-graph diagramming app — Mermaid round-tripping, MP4 cinematic export, Yjs/WebRTC collaboration, multi-provider AI generation, an ELK layout engine and eleven diagram-type plugins. Your instinct that it was “too much itself” was right, but it undersold the problem: it is not a whiteboard, so there was no drag-to-draw gesture to start from. Verified directly against the clone at /home/bam/openflowkit-reference, not from its README.
mechanism:
React Flow edges require a real node id at each end. That is the single fact that makes an Excalidraw-style whiteboard awkward on React Flow: an arrow floating between two bare canvas points has no nodes to connect.

The answer — taken from your own pyblocks board — is to give it some. A free arrow is two invisible 1×1 anchor nodes plus one connector edge. Drop an end inside an existing rectangle and that end binds to the rectangle directly instead of getting an anchor.

The payoff is the bit you can see in the video: because a bound end is a real React Flow edge endpoint, dragging the rectangle moves the arrow with it, for free, with no code of ours involved. The tempting alternative — drawing lines onto a separate SVG overlay above the canvas — would have forfeited stock selection, hit-testing, dragging and z-order, and every one of those would then have been ours to rebuild.

One refinement on top of the donor: a bound end anchors at the shape's centre (the only point that survives a resize) but the visible path is clipped to the shape's border, so an arrow points at a box instead of burying its head inside one. Compare the before and after below.

stock_parts.element: Infinite canvas, pan, zoom, selection, hit-testing
stock_parts.survives: Middle-mouse pans in every tool; left-drag pans only under the Hand tool.
A shape lands where the pointer was, at any pan or zoom.

stock_parts.element: Live preview while dragging out a shape
stock_parts.survives: Preview is drawn in flow coordinates, so it tracks pan/zoom mid-gesture and never intercepts the pointer.
Endpoints re-derive every render, so a line survives moving or resizing either end.
A 2px line stays clickable — and it now emits the stock react-flow__edge-path class the hand-rolled version silently dropped.

stock_parts.element: Reading a bound node's measured box
stock_parts.survives: Border clipping uses the real measured size, not the size we asked for.

stock_parts.element: Delete key, and cascading an edge when its node goes
stock_parts.survives: Delete and Backspace both work; deleting a rectangle takes its connectors with it.
Stock chrome, stock keyboard and button behaviour.
All three flip per tool from one tool state — the only tool-awareness React Flow needs.
Left exactly as stock. No store, no zustand, no reducer — the board is small enough that React Flow's own state hooks are the whole model layer.
Deliberately not hidden. proOptions.hideAttribution exists; leaving it on is the courtesy that keeps the MIT story clean.

shots: Empty board. Viewport is identity — no fitView, because every screen-to-flow assumption in the test suite rests on it.
R pressed: the Rectangle tool is armed and the cursor is a crosshair.
Two rectangles, each drawn at its dragged size. The tool reverted to Select after each one.
A, dragged from inside one rectangle to inside the other: both ends bound, no anchors created, and the path clipped to each border.
L on empty canvas: a headless line on two invisible anchors, reaching its exact drawn endpoints.
The payoff — the top rectangle was dragged and the bound arrow followed it, re-clipping against the new border. No code of ours runs here.
The free line selected and deleted. Both of its anchors went with it; the board is back to two shapes and one arrow.

provenance.source: createAnchorNode and cleanupUnusedAnchors port pyblocks/src/whiteboard/model.ts (createAnchor, and the surviving-reference sweep). normaliseRect and the node constructors are ours, ad hoc.

The v/h/r/l/a table is the five relevant rows of pyblocks/src/whiteboard/bindings.ts:24-58 (DEFAULT_HOTKEYS). The donor's modifier-combo serialisation and per-user rebinding are deliberately left behind.

The gesture shape and screen→flow→commit flow port pyblocks/src/App.tsx onToolPointerDown/onToolPointerMove/createConnector. shapeAt is ours and deliberately not a port — the donor's findSnap/nearestBorderSnap is a zoom-scaled border-proximity system; this board only needs a containment test.
The per-tool <ReactFlow> prop mapping ports pyblocks/src/App.tsx. onDelete and nodeDragThreshold={0} are ours, derived from reading the installed @xyflow/react / @xyflow/system bundles.

Ours. Derived from reading getEdgePosition in the installed @xyflow/system: an edge endpoint's position comes only from a registered <Handle>'s measured bounds, so a node without one renders no edge at all.

Ours, derived from scratch — the standard parametric ray/AABB clip. React Flow's own floating-edges example solves the same problem differently; it was not read or copied, and neither is it an analogue of the donor's border-snap.
Stock <BaseEdge> and getStraightPath. The arrowhead marker is ours, ad hoc.
Evaluated and rejected as a source: no drag-to-draw gesture and no freeform arrows. Recorded so nobody re-checks it.

decisions.q: The repo is public. Say the word if you want it private.
decisions.a: zacharyyamaoka/simple-reactflow-whiteboard, MIT, matching pyblocks/systemsketch/bbox-ui. An MIT whiteboard that nobody can see does not do the job you described. Default if you say nothing: it stays public. One command flips it.

decisions.q: What goes in next — and I'd argue it is not more shapes.
decisions.a: Ellipse, text and freedraw are each an afternoon and none of them teach you anything. Undo/redo is the thing that decides whether this is usable, and it is the thing tldraw gives you for free that React Flow does not. Default if you say nothing: I build undo/redo next, then persistence to a file. Say “shapes first” and I'll flip the order.

decisions.q: Is this meant to become the canvas under SystemSketch, or stay a toy?
decisions.a: This is the strategic question under “an MIT version whiteboard”, and it changes what gets built. If it is a tldraw replacement, the next work is the boring load-bearing half — undo, persistence, copy/paste, z-order — and porting the rest of the pyblocks board is the cheapest route. If it stays a reference implementation, it is already done. I am not assuming either; nothing here forecloses the choice.

decisions.q: What I deliberately did not do.
decisions.a: No ellipse, text, freehand, styling, undo/redo, persistence, copy/paste, groups, frames, ports, or elbow routing — you asked for rectangles and lines/arrows on R, L, A, and widening that quietly would have buried the one mechanism worth reviewing. I also did not touch pyblocks, and did not merge anything anywhere.

footer: Built 2026-09-18. Implementation by a Sonnet builder against assertions written first; audited by a different model, read-only, which found nine defects; fixed and re-verified. Every capture on this page comes from the running app at 127.0.0.1:5199 — none of it is illustration. Sources: /home/bam/simple-reactflow-whiteboard, donor /home/bam/pyblocks/src/whiteboard/, rejected reference /home/bam/openflowkit-reference.
audit:
#What it foundWhy it matteredStatus
1An arrow drawn wholly inside one rectangle became a zero-length edge — invisible, unclickable, and silently accumulating in the model.A completely natural gesture produced silence. You could not see it, select it or delete it.Fixed
2A connector between overlapping or nested shapes collapsed. A ~380px arrow rendered as a 36×40 stub pointing the wrong way; concentric shapes rendered nothing at all.My own border-clipping code: the comment said “leave it alone” and the code returned the other endpoint.Fixed
3With any draw tool armed, the zoom buttons were dead — and pressing R then clicking one dropped a stray rectangle at (-52, 644), off-canvas.The gesture handler sat on <ReactFlow>, and <Controls> is its child.Fixed
4Esc mid-drag flipped the tool but still committed the shape, and left the preview on screen. A real pointercancel committed too.Excalidraw is the stated reference, and there Esc aborts.Fixed
5A free arrow endpoint was documented as draggable but had a zero-pixel grab target. Measured: a 1px miss fails; a miss starts a rubber band across your drawing.The comment claimed a capability that did not exist.Fixed
6The click-vs-drag threshold was measured in flow units, not screen pixels, so it meant 2px zoomed out and 8px zoomed in.A gesture threshold is a statement about your hand, not about the canvas.Fixed
7The anchor-sweep comment asserted that onDelete fires before React Flow applies removals. It fires last.The code was right for a different reason. A plausible-but-false rationale survives review and gets someone later.Comment corrected
8A second pointer silently stole an in-flight gesture; window.__WB__ shipped in the production bundle.Latent, touch-only and a stray handle respectively.Fixed
9The provenance doc had no entry for the one file doing real math, and its ConnectorEdge entry described deleted code.Your standing rule. A citation pointing at the wrong lines is worse than none.Corrected

Two decisions it cleared, with evidence

nodeDragThreshold={0} is a real fix, not a fudge. React Flow's default of 1px anchors a drag at the first move event that crosses the threshold, so whatever distance the pointer covered before that is dropped. The auditor A/B'd it in the browser without touching the repo: the same gesture lands at (400,300) shipped and (388,288) at the default. The shortfall is exactly one input event's displacement at any granularity — 100px at 1 event, 1px at 64 — so a real mouse loses the same way on a fast flick. Cost of 0: a click that slips ≥2px now nudges the shape by that slip. Click-to-select still works.

Every provenance citation into pyblocks was opened and checked. model.ts:377-396, model.ts:944-947, bindings.ts:24-58, App.tsx createConnector, findSnap/nearestBorderSnap and the per-tool prop block all landed exactly where claimed. Two were off by a few lines and are corrected.
